p.src: Complex Numbers in Polar Form

u.src: Complex Numbers in Polar Form
en: Complex Numbers in Polar Form

p.src:
Begin by removing one small source of algebraic friction. A complex number $z=x+iy$ is a point in the complex plane, with $x$ on the real axis and $y$ on the imaginary axis. If the point has polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$, then $x=r\cos\theta,
  \qquad
  y=r\sin\theta,$ and therefore $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=re^{i\theta}.$ Euler’s notation is useful because the angle-addition formulas become the exponential law $e^{i\theta}e^{i\phi}
  =e^{i(\theta+\phi)}.$ Indeed, multiplying the two trigonometric forms gives $\begin{aligned}
& (\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)(\cos\phi+i\sin\phi)
\notag\\
&\qquad=\cos(\theta+\phi)+i\sin(\theta+\phi).\end{aligned}$ The familiar sum formulas are all contained in this one multiplication.

p.src:
Complex conjugation reflects the point across the real axis: $z^*=x-iy,
  \qquad
  (e^{i\theta})^*=e^{-i\theta}.$ Consequently, $e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=1.$ Numbers of the form $e^{i\theta}$ lie on the unit circle and are called pure phases. Every nonzero complex number is a positive modulus times a pure phase: $z=|z|e^{i\theta},
  \qquad
  |z|^2=z^*z=x^2+y^2.$

p.src: Quantum Mechanics as a Probability Calculus

u.src: Quantum Mechanics as a Probability Calculus
en: Quantum Mechanics as a Probability Calculus

p.src: We now turn to the postulates. A physical system is prepared in a state; a measurement asks for the value of an observable; quantum mechanics supplies probabilities for the possible answers.

u.src: We now turn to the postulates. A physical system is prepared in a state; a measurement asks for the value of an observable; quantum mechanics supplies probabilities for the possible answers.
en: We now turn to the postulates. A physical system is prepared in a state; a measurement asks for the value of an observable; quantum mechanics supplies probabilities for the possible answers.

p.src:
States are vectors in a complex vector space. For a two-level spin system, $\ket\psi=\alpha\ket{u}+\beta\ket{d},
  \qquad
  \ket{u}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \ket{d}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$ The coefficients determine the up/down probabilities, $P(u)=|\alpha|^2,
  \qquad
  P(d)=|\beta|^2,$ so the state must be normalized: $\braket{\psi}{\psi}
  =|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2
  =1.$ The dimension refers to the number of independent alternatives in the state space, not to the dimension of ordinary space. A system with three mutually exclusive basis states would use three orthonormal columns and three amplitudes.

Multiplication by a pure phase leaves a magnitude unchanged: $|e^{i\theta}\alpha|^2=|\alpha|^2.$ The amplitudes therefore contain information beyond the probabilities for this one basis. Its role will become visible when different measurements and, later, time evolution are considered.

p.src: Why Observables Are Hermitian

u.src: Why Observables Are Hermitian
en: Why Observables Are Hermitian

p.src: Experimental results can be recorded as real numbers. We may package two real numbers into one complex number for convenience, but the pointer readings themselves can always be separated into real quantities. In finite dimensions, quantum observables are represented by a special class of linear operators: Hermitian matrices.

In finite dimensions, quantum observables are represented by a special class of linear operators: Hermitian matrices.
en: Experimental results can be recorded as real numbers. We may package two real numbers into one complex number for convenience, but the pointer readings themselves can always be separated into real quantities. In finite dimensions, quantum observables are represented by a special class of linear operators: Hermitian matrices.

p.src:
To define them, first transpose a matrix by interchanging rows and columns: $(M^T)_{ij}=M_{ji}.$ A real matrix satisfying $M^T=M$ is symmetric. For complex matrices the corresponding operation is the Hermitian conjugate, $M^\dagger=(M^T)^*,
  \qquad
  (M^\dagger)_{ij}=M_{ji}^*.$

p.src:
A matrix $M$ is Hermitian if $M^\dagger=M,
  \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
  M_{ij}=M_{ji}^*.$

p.src:
The diagonal entries are real, since $M_{ii}=M_{ii}^*$. Reflected off-diagonal entries are conjugate pairs. Thus the general two-by-two form is $M=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    a&z\\
    z^*&b
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad a,b\in\mathbb R.$ Hermiticity is the matrix analogue of a reality condition; it does not require every entry separately to be real.

p.src:
The first payoff follows from two elementary conjugation identities: $\braket{B}{A}=\braket{A}{B}^*,$ and, for any $M$, $\bra B M\ket A
  =
  \bigl(\bra A M^\dagger\ket B\bigr)^*.$ The expression $\bra B M\ket A$ is a number, the $BA$ matrix element of $M$. If $M$ is Hermitian and $B=A$, then $\bra A M\ket A
  =
  \bigl(\bra A M\ket A\bigr)^*.$ It is therefore real.

p.src:
For a Hermitian matrix the eigenvalue is real. Multiplying Equation  on the left by $\bra a$ gives $\bra a M\ket a
  =\lambda_a\braket{a}{a}.$ The left side is real by Hermiticity, and the norm on the right is real and positive. Hence $\lambda_a
  =
  \frac{\bra a M\ket a}{\braket{a}{a}}
  \in\mathbb R.$

u.src: The Three Spin Matrices
en: The Three Spin Matrices

p.src:
For electron spin along the third axis, choose $\sigma_3=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1&0\\
    0&-1
  \end{pmatrix}.$ Its eigenstates are $\ket u=(1,0)^T$ with eigenvalue $+1$ and $\ket d=(0,1)^T$ with eigenvalue $-1$. Thus the two possible detector values are the two eigenvalues.

p.src:
The first-axis spin matrix is $\sigma_1=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    0&1\\
    1&0
  \end{pmatrix}.$ Its candidate eigenvectors are first written without normalization, since multiplying an eigenvector by any nonzero scalar leaves it an eigenvector. Physical states, however, must be normalized: $\begin{aligned}
  \ket{x+}
  &=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
  &
  \sigma_1\ket{x+}&=+\ket{x+},
  \notag\\
  \ket{x-}
  &=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix},
  &
  \sigma_1\ket{x-}&=-\ket{x-}.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src: Before proving the next theorem, state its meaning. If one observable gives two different definite answers in two states, then a measurement of that observable can distinguish the states perfectly. Quantum mechanics expresses this perfect distinguishability as orthogonality.

  \qquad
  M\ket B=\lambda_B\ket B.$ If $\lambda_A\ne\lambda_B$, then $\braket{B}{A}=0.$

p.src: Proof. Multiplying the first eigenvalue equation by $\bra B$ gives $\bra B M\ket A=\lambda_A\braket{B}{A}.$ Hermiticity and the second eigenvalue equation give the same matrix element as $\bra B M\ket A=\lambda_B\braket{B}{A},$ because $\lambda_B$ is real. Subtraction yields $(\lambda_A-\lambda_B)\braket{B}{A}=0.$ The eigenvalues are different, so the inner product must vanish. ◻

p.src: The Probability Postulate

u.src: The Probability Postulate
en: The Probability Postulate

p.src:
Suppose the system is prepared in a normalized state $\ket B$. Let $M$ be an observable, and let $\ket A$ be a normalized eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_A$. Then the probability that measuring $M$ returns $\lambda_A$ is $P(\lambda_A\mid B)
  =
  |\braket{A}{B}|^2
  =
  \braket{A}{B}\braket{B}{A}.$ The product is real and nonnegative. For normalized vectors it is at most one.

Suppose the system is prepared in a normalized state $\ket B$. Let $M$ be an observable, and let $\ket A$ be a normalized eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_A$. Then the probability that measuring $M$ returns $\lambda_A$ is $P(\lambda_A\mid B)
  =
  |\braket{A}{B}|^2
  =
  \braket{A}{B}\braket{B}{A}.$ The product is real and nonnegative. For normalized vectors it is at most one.
en:
Suppose the system is prepared in a normalized state $\ket B$. Let $M$ be an observable, and let $\ket A$ be a normalized eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_A$. Then the probability that measuring $M$ returns $\lambda_A$ is $P(\lambda_A\mid B)
  =
  |\braket{A}{B}|^2
  =
  \braket{A}{B}\braket{B}{A}.$ The product is real and nonnegative. For normalized vectors it is at most one.

p.src: The preceding sentence can be misunderstood unless the vocabulary is repaired. A magnetic moment has a spatial direction, which we shall call a pointer. p.src:
Let $\hat n=(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ be a unit pointer in ordinary space: $n_1^2+n_2^2+n_3^2=1.$ The operator for spin along that direction is the matrix-valued analogue of a dot product: $\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\hat n
  =
  n_1\sigma_1+n_2\sigma_2+n_3\sigma_3
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    n_3&n_1-in_2\\
    n_1+in_2&-n_3
  \end{pmatrix}.$ It is Hermitian: the diagonal entries are real and the off-diagonal entries are conjugates.

p.src:
To find its possible values, square it before inserting matrix entries. Matrix order matters, so the cross terms occur as anticommutators: $\begin{aligned}
  (\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\hat n)^2
  &=
  n_1^2\sigma_1^2+n_2^2\sigma_2^2+n_3^2\sigma_3^2
  \notag\\
  &\quad
  +n_1n_2(\sigma_1\sigma_2+\sigma_2\sigma_1)
  \notag\\
  &\quad
  +n_2n_3(\sigma_2\sigma_3+\sigma_3\sigma_2)
  \notag\\
  &\quad
  +n_1n_3(\sigma_1\sigma_3+\sigma_3\sigma_1).
  \end{aligned}$ Different Pauli matrices anticommute: $\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=0
  \qquad(i\ne j).$ The lecture checks one case explicitly: $\sigma_1\sigma_3
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \sigma_3\sigma_1
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
  =-\sigma_1\sigma_3.$

p.src:
The cross terms in Equation  vanish, while $\sigma_i^2=I$. Hence $(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\hat n)^2
  =(n_1^2+n_2^2+n_3^2)I
  =I.$ Every eigenvalue therefore satisfies $\lambda^2=1$: $\lambda=\pm1.$ Whichever spatial axis the apparatus selects, the detector still has only the two outcomes $+1$ and $-1$. The relation between nearby directions appears not as an intermediate measured value, but in the probabilities of those two fixed answers.
